title: Parametric Prior Mapping for Time Series
one_liner: Combine a simple initial prediction with a flexible neural network to forecast future values while honestly measuring uncertainty.
lead: When forecasting future values in a time series (like stock prices or weather), you need both an accurate point estimate and an honest uncertainty band. Deep neural networks can learn complex patterns but often give overconfident predictions. Parametric methods (using fixed probability models) are honest but too rigid. This paper shows how to start with a simple parametric guess and then route it through a neural network to get both benefits: accuracy and genuine uncertainty.

paras: A time series forecaster needs two things: a good point estimate (the single best guess for tomorrow's value) and an honest uncertainty estimate (how far off that guess might be). Real data like stock prices or weather do not behave the same way across all time — they are non-stationary, meaning the pattern itself shifts.

Parametric methods (like DeepAR, which assumes all future values follow a fixed bell-shaped probability curve, called a Gaussian, with two numbers that control its center and width) are stable and efficient, but they assume the same probability shape applies everywhere. When reality is non-stationary, they break down. Deep generative models can learn arbitrary patterns, but they are compute-heavy and often give overconfident uncertainty — the predicted confidence bands do not actually match the real error rates.
You are stuck: stay rigid or become expensive and untrustworthy. Neither choice works well.

callout.html: Start with a simple parametric guess for the shape of the uncertainty, then feed that guess through a neural network mapping that adapts it to match the actual data.

steps.text: Feed past values into a neural encoder to create a summary of what happened before.
Use the history summary to compute mean and variance (the two numbers that fully describe a bell-curve guess) for a starting parametric guess (the prior).
Draw a few random samples from that starting guess to make concrete initial predictions.
Feed each sample through a neural network that transforms them to match the true data distribution.
Use the final samples to estimate density, compute loss, and train both the encoder and the mapping.

paras: The paper changes the starting prior distribution — the initial guess for what shape the uncertainty takes. Instead of a fixed, hand-chosen bell curve, the prior is now computed dynamically from the actual data via a parametric estimator.

hidden.name: Mutual information between input and hidden numbers in the prior
paras: The paper introduces and measures how much of the input's information flows into the starting guess. If you extract information about the current state and encode it into the prior (rather than just using a fixed formula), that prior becomes more context-aware and more likely to land close to the real distribution. This is measured as mutual information: a number that goes up when the prior knows more about the input. High mutual information means the prior already carries clues from the input, not generic assumptions.

The paper estimates this using the mutual-information lower bound, computed on the test data. Higher mutual information means the starting prior is richer and more reliable because it carries knowledge from the input. When the neural mapping starts from a prior that already knows about the input, it has less distance to travel to the true answer, so it trains faster and stays stable (no thrashing or collapse).

heat.caption: Darker means more information from input in the prior. Steady high values mean stable learning.

reads.html: The starting guess (prior) should carry as much real-world context as possible, because a smarter first guess makes the neural mapping's job easier and more stable.

Mutual-information lower bound between input x and the hidden samples z (drawn from the prior) measures how much conditional information the parametric prior preserves from the input, serving as a proxy for prior quality.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the two-layer combination
paras: The mechanism rests on splitting the job into two layers. The parametric layer (mean and variance computed directly from the data using a fast formula) is cheap, stable, and data-driven but limited in shape. The neural layer (the mapping that pushes samples forward) is flexible and can learn any transformation but needs a good starting point to train reliably.

By starting with a parametric prior that is context-aware (computed fresh for each input, not fixed globally), you give the neural mapping a warm start: the prior is already close to the true distribution on average, so the network does not have to search the entire possibility space from scratch. This reduces overfitting because the network learns small refinements rather than building from scratch, making the learning process stable and reliable. The hybrid loss (combining likelihood loss and mean-squared-error loss) reinforces this: the likelihood loss shapes the distribution's tails (where uncertainty lives), while the MSE loss anchors the center to the true mean, preventing the network from drifting into overconfident fantasy.

In non-stationary data where the pattern keeps changing, this matters more. A global fixed prior (like standard parametric methods) assumes the same shape always applies — false. A pure neural network without a prior has no inductive bias and can learn gibberish. PPM gives you an inductive bias that updates per input, the best of both worlds.

stages.s: Encoder extracts what the history reveals
Parametric prior computes starting guess (mean, width)
Draw samples from the starting guess
Neural mapping bends samples to match reality
Density estimation counts samples at each value

math.h2: The loss function that trains it
math.words: Total loss equals negative log-likelihood of the forecast distribution (how closely predicted densities match actual outcomes), plus a weighted mean-squared-error term anchoring the forecast mean to the data mean.
symbols: Negative log-likelihood loss (how closely the predicted probability density matches the actual outcome; lower is better)
Mean-squared-error loss (how far the predicted mean drifts from the true mean)
Weight controlling how much we care about mean accuracy versus distribution shape (set to 0.1)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose at time step t the true next value is 100.
Predicted distribution has mean 99, std dev 5 (so density at 100 is high). NLL-loss for this step: 0.8.
Same forecast, but MSE-term compares predicted mean 99 to true mean 100: (99-100)^2 = 1. MSE-loss: 1.
Total: L_total = 0.8 + 0.1*1 = 0.9. Both terms pull learning in the same direction (accurate mean, accurate shape).
If α=0 (ignore MSE), the network might drift the mean away and stay high-likelihood by widening std dev (overconfident bands).
If α=1.0 (too heavy on MSE), the network learns to squash all variance and predict a point, losing uncertainty.
α=0.1 balances them: distribution shape matters most, but mean stays anchored.

math.note: The hybrid objective prevents two failure modes: pure likelihood can overfit to the tail at the cost of mean accuracy, and pure MSE ignores uncertainty calibration entirely.

bars.h2: How it compares on held-out data

charts.title: Rigid parametric baseline
charts.note: Fast and cheap, but inaccurate and overconfident.

charts.title: Pure neural generative model
charts.note: More accurate but gives false certainty because the neural network learns to squeeze high probability mass onto the observed outcome, leaving narrow bands that rarely contain future values, making the confidence intervals untrustworthy. It also requires heavy computation because training and inference both run many neural forward passes.

charts.title: PPM (this paper)
charts.note: Wins the trade-off: nearly as accurate as the pure network, far more honest on uncertainty, almost as fast as the baseline.

items.b: The prior misses the mark entirely at training start.
items.html: If the parametric formula (e.g., sample mean and variance from the first 10 steps) does not match the true pattern, the prior is so far from the true distribution that the mapping must do too much work, causing training to stall or diverge. Fix: seed the prior estimation with more data or warm-start the encoder.

If the MSE weight is too large, the network learns to ignore distribution shape and predict a tight point estimate, losing all uncertainty. If the MSE weight is too small, the forecast mean drifts away from the true value while the network stays overconfident by widening the predicted variance band. Fix: tune the weight on a validation set to find the balance.

items.b: Non-stationary data shifts so fast the prior cannot adapt.
items.html: If the distribution's shape changes faster than the encoder can learn new context, the prior stays stale because it reflects a weighted average of the input over the full context window, including old data that no longer matches the current moment. The mapping then stretches an outdated starting guess, and the forecast learns yesterday's pattern instead because the network cannot catch up in one pass. Fix: shorten the context window so the encoder focuses on recent data, or use a technique that puts more weight on recent history than old history.

items.b: Done right: architecture and loss align.
items.html: When the parametric prior is context-aware (encoder feeds it real history), hybrid loss balances mean and shape, and the mapping is given enough capacity, PPM delivers accurate forecasts with confidence bands that match the true error rates — the goal of the paper.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple time series (e.g., mixture of sine waves with time-varying amplitude to simulate non-stationarity). Train PPM and a baseline parametric method on the first 80% of the data. On the held-out last 20%, compute two metrics: (1) how far the point forecast is from the true value (MAE), and (2) how often the true value falls within the predicted 80% confidence interval. A parametric baseline will have either low MAE but bad calibration (true values fall outside the bands too often) or good calibration with poor accuracy. PPM improves both because the adaptive prior keeps the starting guess close to the moving target, and the hybrid loss prevents the network from sacrificing either accuracy or uncertainty calibration to chase the other.
demo.metric_eq: Calibration = (count of true values inside 80% bands) / (total predictions); ideal = 0.8. MAE = average absolute difference between forecast and true value.
demo.closing: What should become impossible to miss: as data becomes more non-stationary (the pattern shifts more), a rigid parametric prior falls further behind because it assumes a fixed shape. PPM's adaptive prior, computed fresh for each input, follows the shifts and keeps both accuracy and calibration high across all regimes.
